You leave at ten again, and the volunteers no longer look up when the lift doors close.
Your speech is the best-prepared in the House, and the Tuesday queue is a little longer for it.
The volunteers keep a list of the residents who asked for you after ten, and give it to you monthly.

variants.title: Meet-the-People, After the Rain
variants.body: A downpour at seven, so everyone comes at nine. The queue includes a family whose flat appeal has been turned down twice, and a man who would like the void deck named after his father. The House sits at noon.

choices.text: Stay until the last one is seen.
choices.outcome: Past one in the morning. The void deck will not be renamed, and you tell him so kindly enough that he shakes your hand twice. You read your papers for the sitting in the car.

choices.text: Take the family's appeal, and write it yourself.
choices.outcome: Two pages, citing the right paragraph. The appeal succeeds on the third try, which the family credits to persistence and you credit to the paragraph. The void deck man is seen by a volunteer.

choices.text: Leave the volunteers to finish. Read your papers.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten and are word-perfect in the House. The volunteers stay until one. The following Tuesday, the void deck man asks, pointedly, whether you are staying tonight.

variants.title: Tuesday Night, the Lift
variants.body: Thirty residents and one theme: a lift that has been under upgrading for eleven months. Nobody is angry with you. Everybody would like you to be angry on their behalf, tonight, in person.

choices.text: See every one of them, one by one.
choices.outcome: Thirty conversations about the same lift, until one in the morning. They go home feeling heard, which is not a lift but is not nothing.

choices.text: Write about the lift properly, tonight.
choices.outcome: Your letter names the contractor, the start date and the eleven months. A new completion date arrives within the week and is met. The residents were seen by volunteers, and noticed.

choices.text: Let the volunteers take the rest.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten to prepare for the House. Twenty-nine residents are seen about the lift. The thirtieth wanted you, and mentions it at every block party for a year.

title: The Walkabout
body: Wet market, 7:20am, a camera crew, and a stallholder with strong and specific views about the price of chillies, which she is delighted to share at volume. Fourteen stalls are still to go.

choices.text: Listen to her properly, on camera.
choices.outcome: Four minutes of her talking and you not interrupting. The clip is shared widely, and the comments are, unusually, kind. The last fourteen stalls get nine seconds each.

choices.text: Keep moving. Every stall gets a handshake.
choices.outcome: Nineteen stalls in forty minutes. The photographs are excellent and no one remembers a word.

choices.text: Take her number. Call her tonight, off camera.
choices.outcome: You call at nine. She talks for forty minutes about chillies, supply chains and her nephew. None of it is filmed, and two of her points end up in a letter to the ministry.

0: Wet markets at 7am, with cameras, until you know the price of chillies better than the price of anything else.
An auntie says you looked thinner on television, and you listen to the rest, which is about the lift.
A stallholder you once listened to on camera now greets you with the price of something new.
Another walkabout, another auntie, and four minutes of footage about the lift, which the news runs in full.
A fishmonger explains the price of fish to you on camera, and the clip is shared mostly by fishmongers.
You hear out a complaint about a bus route on camera, and the route is changed, though not because of the camera.
1: A walkabout in the rain, on schedule, and the photograph of you under someone else's umbrella does very well.
Eleven stalls in forty minutes: everyone gets a handshake and nobody gets a sentence.
Fourteen stalls, fourteen handshakes and a volunteer one step behind you with hand sanitiser.
The walkabout keeps to time and the photographs are excellent, and nobody remembers a word you said.
Every stall gets a handshake before nine, and you are in the car by a quarter past, as planned.
The walkabout is so punctual that the stallholders now time their breaks by it.
2: You take numbers at walkabouts and call them at night, and your call log becomes the best map of the ward.
Three phone numbers on a napkin from the wet market, and you call all three that evening, off camera.
You call a stallholder back about her rent, and she tells the next stall, and the next.
A resident you called at night tells the RC, which now knows you mainly for that.
Your evening calls now take longer than the walkabouts, and settle more.
A hawker you called back about her lease tells you the next week that it was renewed, as if you did it.

variants.title: The Hawker Centre
variants.body: Lunchtime at a hawker centre, with photographers. The uncle at the drinks stall would like to explain, in detail, why his rent has gone up and what he thinks should be done about it.

choices.text: Sit down and hear him out.
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes, one kopi going cold, and a follow-up on his rent in writing. The one photographer who stayed gets the best picture of the day. The next three stalls get none.

choices.text: Buy a kopi, smile, and keep moving.
choices.outcome: You pay for the kopi, smile for the photograph and move on. In the photograph, he is still talking.

choices.text: Ask for his number. Call him tonight.
choices.outcome: You call after dinner. He has prepared notes. His rent goes to the agency under your name the next morning, and there is no photograph of any of it.

variants.title: The Estate Visit
variants.body: Eight blocks before lunch and a ribbon to cut. A resident on a mobility scooter would like to show you a ramp that does not quite reach the kerb.

choices.text: Go and look at the ramp.
choices.outcome: You walk the ramp with her, slowly, cameras behind you. It is two centimetres short, and fixed within a fortnight. The ribbon is cut forty minutes late, to applause from people who wanted lunch.

choices.text: Promise someone will look, and stay on schedule.
choices.outcome: Someone does look, eventually. The ribbon is cut on time, by you, in a photograph that is very well lit.

choices.text: Get her number. Send someone this afternoon.
choices.outcome: An officer measures the ramp at four: two centimetres short. It is fixed within a fortnight. She sends you a photograph of herself using it, and nobody else ever sees it.

title: The Parliamentary Question
body: Filed for oral answer: a good question, sharply drafted, about a scheme your ministry runs. The honest answer is not flattering. The brief your officials wrote is accurate, and answers a slightly different question.

choices.text: Answer it straight, and say what you will do.
choices.outcome: You concede the point and say what you are doing about it. The supplementary is gentler than it would have been, because there is nothing left to prise open.

choices.text: Read the brief, which answers a nearby question.
choices.outcome: Technically responsive, substantively elsewhere. It is a skill, you are good at it, and the clip will be on the internet for longer than the scheme.

choices.text: Promise a full written answer, and write it properly.
choices.outcome: The written answer runs to four pages, with tables, and is the most complete account the ministry has given of the scheme. The Member reads it. So does one researcher.

0: At Question Time you answer the question that was asked, which is still noticed.
Seven questions this sitting, and two of your answers make the news for being short and true.
A Member files a question expecting a brief, gets an answer instead, and files another.
Your straight answers are now quoted back to you in supplementaries, so somebody read them.
You give the House the actual number, and the Member who asked has no supplementary ready.
Your answer is one paragraph shorter than the brief, and it is the paragraph that dodged.
1: At Question Time you answer a question that was nearly the one asked.
A sharp supplementary meets a smooth reply; Hansard records both, and the papers record the reply.
Question Time again, and the brief answers a question your officials found easier.
Your replies this sitting are smooth enough that the supplementaries slide straight off them.
The brief is read in full, accurately, and a Member asks the original question again in other words.
You read the brief so well that nobody can quite say which question it answered.
2: Seven questions this sitting, and the full written answers follow, as promised, with tables.
Another four-page written answer, and a university researcher cites three of them in a paper, with footnotes.
Another written answer arrives, longer than the question and shorter than its annex.
Your written answers come with tables, and one Member starts filing questions just to get them.
Your written answer is footnoted so thoroughly that the Member who asked thanks you for the reading list.
Another question becomes another written answer, delivered on the date you promised, which is the news.

variants.title: Question Time
variants.body: A Member asks whether the ministry will review a rule that residents raise at every Meet-the-People Session. It is being reviewed. Nothing has been decided, and an announcement is planned for March, with a backdrop.

choices.text: Say it is under review, and what is being looked at.
choices.outcome: You say so, plainly, with the three things being looked at. The Member thanks you. The announcement in March makes smaller news than it would have, backdrop and all.

choices.text: Say the ministry keeps all its rules under review.
choices.outcome: This is true of every rule and says nothing about this one. The Member points that out. Hansard records you both, and the announcement in March gets the headline.

choices.text: Offer the Member a full written reply once it is decided.
choices.outcome: The written reply goes out the week after the decision: three pages, complete. The Member reads all of it, and files a new question about the parts the announcement left out.

variants.title: The Supplementary
variants.body: Your answer to the question went well. The Member rises for a supplementary, and it is the one your officials said would not come. The brief has nothing on it.

choices.text: Answer it straight, without the brief.
choices.outcome: You say you do not have the figure to hand, then say what you do know, which is enough. Your officials send a note that reads, in full, "Well handled."

choices.text: Answer a nearby question the brief does cover.
choices.outcome: The answer is fluent, confident and about something else. The Member says, "That was not my question," and is quoted the next morning in full.

choices.text: Offer to write to the Member, and do it properly.
choices.outcome: You write two pages, with the figure you did not have to hand. The Member quotes your letter in the next debate, more kindly than you had expected.

title: The Ministry Townhall
body: Four hundred officers. The anonymous question board has one item upvoted far beyond the rest, and it is about workload and it is not polite.

choices.text: Read it out and answer it.
choices.outcome: You read it in full, including the rude part, and then you answer it for eleven minutes without notes. The room changes temperature. It is the only thing from that townhall anybody repeats. It is noted.

choices.text: Address the theme without reading it.
choices.outcome: You speak warmly about wellbeing and the importance of sustainable pace. Four hundred officers understand precisely what has happened.

0: The top question is about workload again, you read it out again, and the upvotes stop being anonymous in spirit.
Four hundred officers, one microphone and a rude question read out in full, which is the only part anyone repeats.
An officer thanks you at the lift for reading the rude question out, in a whisper, in case it counts.
You read the top question out in full, and the next year one officer signs her name to hers.
The question about workload is read out again, and this time a director in the front row nods.
1: The top question is about workload, and you address its theme, warmly.
Your townhall slides circulate, unofficially, as an example of what a townhall can be.
The townhall runs to time and the theme is addressed, while the question waits on the board like a queue number.
Your answer to the theme of the question is warm enough that HR asks to use it in a module.
The theme of the top question becomes the title of next year's townhall, which is one way to answer it.

variants.title: The Curated Questions
variants.body: This year's townhall questions were submitted in advance and curated. An officer at the back puts her hand up anyway.

choices.text: Take her question.
choices.outcome: It is about promotions, and it is fair. You answer it partly, and say that it is partly. Afterwards the curated questions are the part nobody remembers.

choices.text: Say there will be time at the end.
choices.outcome: There is no time at the end. There was never going to be, and four hundred officers watched her lower her hand.

variants.title: The Survey Results
variants.body: The ministry's engagement survey is back. Most numbers went up. One went down a long way: whether officers feel safe raising concerns.

choices.text: Put that number on the first slide.
choices.outcome: The first slide is the bad number, in large type, and you talk about it for ten minutes. Two directors look at the floor. Four hundred officers look at you.

choices.text: Lead with the numbers that went up.
choices.outcome: The deck opens on engagement, up four points. The other number is on slide nineteen. Most of the room found slide nineteen before you started.

title: A Year Without Incident
body: Everything runs. The schemes run. You go to Bintan in June and nothing breaks while you are gone, which is either a compliment or a warning.

choices.text: Use it to fix something nobody asked you to fix.
choices.outcome: You get a process fixed that has annoyed eleven thousand people for a decade. It takes a year and it is never announced.

choices.text: Use it to build your network.
choices.outcome: Coffee, lunches, and a very great deal of being remembered. It is not work. It is, unmistakably, the job.

choices.text: Use it to rest.
choices.outcome: You rest. It turns out you needed it more than the ministry needed the other two options.

0: Nothing breaks all year, which you suspect is not a coincidence and cannot prove.
You use a quiet year to fix a process that annoyed people since before you arrived, and never announce it.
You spend a quiet year fixing a form nobody asked you to fix, and three people quietly stop complaining.
A quiet year, and you clear a backlog that predates three directors, without telling any of them.
You fix the meeting-room booking system in a quiet year, and the queue for the big room quietly disappears.
In a quiet year you write down a process that existed only in one retiring officer's head.
1: A quiet year and forty lunches, thirty of which you remember, which is about average.
You attend everything you are invited to, and by December you are invited to more.
A quiet year of coffees in the same three cafés, with people who will remember you as "helpful".
A quiet year of networking, after which three people you have met once describe you as "a friend".
In a quiet year you join two committees, both for the networking and one of them for the food.
A quiet year of receptions, where you learn to hold a plate, a glass and a business card at once.
2: Bintan in June, where you check your email only twice, which is progress.
A quiet year, and somewhere someone writes "steady" about you and means it kindly.
A quiet year, and you take all your leave, which HR's system flags as unusual.
You rest, and the schemes keep running without you, which is reassuring and very slightly insulting.
A quiet year, and you leave at six without a single email asking where you are.
A quiet year, and you read three books, none of them about leadership.

variants.body: No crisis, no reorganisation, no parliamentary question with your name in it. Your diary has white space for the first time in years, and everyone around you has noticed, and is pretending not to.

choices.text: Use it to fix something small and permanent.
choices.outcome: You fix the thing that has made every new joiner's first week worse for a decade. Nobody thanks you. The new joiners never find out what it used to be like.

choices.text: Use it for the lunches you keep postponing.
choices.outcome: Eleven lunches, four dinners and one kopi at a hawker centre that turns out to matter more than the dinners. People remember you now in a way they did not.

choices.text: Use it to sleep.
choices.outcome: You sleep. Your doctor, who has been saying things for three years, says nothing, which is the nicest thing a doctor has ever said to you.

variants.body: Nothing much happens to you this year. The most discussed thing on your floor is the new coffee machine, which has nine settings; everyone uses the same one. A quiet year is a chance to do something for yourself.

choices.text: Read every file you've been forwarded and never opened.
choices.outcome: In the unopened files you find two problems you can fix, and one that someone should have fixed three years ago. You fix the two, and write a note about the third that nobody will enjoy receiving.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the people who decide things.
choices.outcome: You become the person who knows where everything is and who to ask. It isn't a title, but it gets you into rooms.

choices.text: Take your leave, all of it.
choices.outcome: You take every day of leave you're owed. The office copes without you, which is either reassuring or not.

title: The Counter
body: You're a Management Executive at the {ministry}, eight months in. Before this you spent four years working a public service counter, and you're still finishing a part-time degree at night. Your reporting officer, {senior}, has set up a team to redesign how the public applies for a scheme. You're the most junior person on it, and the only one who has ever worked a counter.

choices.text: Tell the team exactly why the new design will fail.
choices.outcome: You describe, from memory, the eleven things a person at a counter is actually holding in their hands. The room goes quiet, and the design changes. {senior} asks where you worked before, and listens to the whole answer.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the pilot show them.
choices.outcome: The pilot fails exactly the way you knew it would, and you're the one asked to fix it. Being listened to the first time would have been less work.

title: The Last Paper
body: Your part-time degree is down to one Saturday exam, after six years of evening classes. It's also the busiest month of the year at work. {peer}, who joined the service the same year as you, finished {peer.their} degree at twenty-two, full-time, on a scholarship. Finishing yours opens jobs a diploma doesn't.

choices.text: Sit the exam and finish it.
choices.outcome: Second Upper. Nobody at work marks it, because nobody at work knew. But it changes which jobs you can apply for, and, more slowly, which ones you think you can.

choices.text: Defer it. Work needs you this month.
choices.outcome: The busy month is followed by another, and another. You finish the degree four years later, by which time the jobs it would have opened have gone to other people.

title: Someone From Before
body: At an inter-agency meeting you recognise the chair. Years ago, before the degree, you sat two desks apart at the same statutory board, on the same grade.

choices.text: Speak to her afterwards.
choices.outcome: She remembers you immediately and without condescension, which you had not dared expect. She puts you on two committees that matter and tells you, plainly, which one to care about.

choices.text: Say nothing. She has moved on.
choices.outcome: She has not moved on; she simply did not see you. You think about the two desks for a week afterwards and then you stop.

title: The Board Takes a Second Look
body: A promotion board has been asked, unusually, to revisit an officer whose record does not match their grade. The officer is you.

choices.text: Make the case yourself, in writing.
choices.outcome: Four pages. You do not argue that you have been treated unfairly, which would have been true and useless; you argue what you would do with the next grade. The estimate is revised. Nobody tells you by how much.

choices.text: Let the record speak.
choices.outcome: The record does speak, and it is a good record, and it moves them slightly less than four pages would have.

title: The Figure, Cited
body: A review of the scheme's design cites a utilisation rate of 31%, attributed to a slide from your division. {Asker} asks, carefully, who presented it.

options.text: {senior}, who once asked you for a range,

choices.text: Say it was you.
choices.outcome: {Asker.short} nods slowly. You watch your name move from one column of something to another.

choices.text: Say it was a team effort.
choices.outcome: It was not, entirely. Your team knows that, and it does you more good with them than the other answer would have done upstairs.

title: Paragraph Four
body: The consultancy's recommendations have been implemented, and have failed in exactly the way your minute paper, two years older, predicted in paragraph four. Someone has found paragraph four.

choices.text: Let paragraph four speak for itself.
choices.outcome: It is read aloud at a meeting you are not at. Afterwards, three people forward it to you, each believing they are the first.

choices.text: Offer to fix it.
choices.outcome: They let you. It takes a year, and a consultancy is engaged to evaluate your fix.

title: The Thing Nobody Announced
body: Every ministry that announced something at COS is now explaining delays. Your Minister, who announced nothing, is the only one who is not. He has noticed.

choices.text: Bring him the pilot, now that it is ready.
choices.outcome: He announces it at the next COS, on time and as described. He mentions your division by name, which Ministers do not do.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let him draw the conclusion.
choices.outcome: He draws it. When his Permanent Secretary next asks which divisions he rates, yours is the first he names, in front of the person who writes your ranking.

title: The Raw Feedback
body: A think tank has analysed the raw feedback you published. Its paper is cited in Parliament, approvingly, by both sides. Your Permanent Secretary forwards it to you with no comment, which from her is a great deal of comment.

choices.text: Reply with one line.
choices.outcome: "Thank you. It was their feedback." She replies within a minute, which nobody has ever seen her do.

choices.text: Write the follow-up nobody asked for.
choices.outcome: It becomes the template for the next national conversation, which uses four pillars.

title: The Decision Paper
body: The Inter-Ministry Committee has been dissolved. Its replacement has adopted your decision paper as its terms of reference, and someone has left your name in the footer.

choices.text: Leave your name on it.
choices.outcome: The footer travels further than you ever have. A Deputy Secretary you have never met asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it off before it circulates.
choices.outcome: It circulates anonymously, which in this building is how people find out who wrote it.

title: The Third Point
body: The scheme has been amended, quietly, in exactly the way the third point suggested. {journalist}, {journalist.aTitle} at the paper, notices that you were the only office holder who said so in public.

choices.text: Take the question on the record.
choices.outcome: The piece runs on a Sunday. Its headline uses the word "candid", which your press secretary has asked you never to be again.

choices.text: Credit the post's author.
choices.outcome: He is astonished, then gracious, then a reliable critic for the rest of your career, which is a kind of compliment.

title: Hansard
body: A newer Member quotes you in her own speech, word for word, with attribution. Someone on the front bench looks up the original.

choices.text: Send her a note.
choices.outcome: She frames it. You hear about this from four people, none of whom are her.

choices.text: Say nothing.
choices.outcome: The quote goes round without you. It turns out to be the most-shared thing you have ever said.

title: Terms of Reference
body: A committee has been appointed to review political salaries. Your question in Cabinet appears, unattributed, as item three of its terms of reference.

choices.text: Make a submission under your own name.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for your submission. Its report adjusts the formula by a percentage point, which it describes as significant.

choices.text: Let item three do the work.
choices.outcome: It does very little work. But you were seen not to make a fuss, which is its own kind of item.

title: The Annual Report
body: The statutory board you were sent to fix has published its annual report. For the first time in four years it contains no restatements, and the auditors' letter is one page long.

choices.text: Ask to come back.
choices.outcome: You come back to a better office than the one you left. It turns out the secondment was a proving ground. Nobody tells you this; they simply act as if it had always been obvious.

choices.text: Ask to stay and finish it.
choices.outcome: You stay. The board becomes the case study on the leadership programme, taught by someone who was never there.

title: Polling Day, Again
body: Parliament is dissolved on a Tuesday. Nobody is surprised; the tents went up in the void decks a fortnight ago. This time your branch chairman has started using the word "swing" in sentences about you.

choices.text: Campaign on the record.
choices.outcome: You stand on a lorry and read out numbers. Some of them are your numbers.

choices.text: Walk every block, every night, for nine days.
choices.outcome: Nine nights, four hundred lift lobbies, one pair of shoes you will never wear again.

lines: On the campaign lorry you read out numbers, some of them yours.
The thank-you lorry takes the same route as last time, down to the stop for kopi at the same coffee shop.
Nine days of campaigning, one rally, and a sample count that tells everyone the result before the real one does.
Your ward's result is among the first in, which your branch treats as a personal achievement.
The posters go up at the first permitted minute and come down by the date on the permit.
Cooling-off day: no campaigning, so you spend it reading the comments, which is worse.
Nomination Day, nine days of walkabouts, and a result your branch chairman predicted, in writing, to within a point.
By the end of the campaign you can rank every coffee shop in the ward by its kopi, privately.

title: The Indicators
body: Growth is strong and the forecasts are kind. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets must be settled this month. It will move two of the four indicators that set the National Bonus, yours included.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Growth comes in a little under forecast, which in a strong year is noticed. The commentary uses the word "moderate" four times.

choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast. Incomes at the 20th percentile rise too, slightly, the way a small boat rises when a larger one goes past.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses its target band by a tenth of a point. The chart is still a good chart.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median, which they have not done in six years. The chart goes into the Budget speech, in colour.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Change nothing that is working.
choices.outcome: The targets are met to the decimal place. Nothing is announced, because nothing has changed, and the plan goes round other ministries as a model.

variants.body: Finance writes to every ministry: the good years have room in them. Your Permanent Secretary has drafted three replies on the next three Budgets and stacked them on your desk, in an order that is a recommendation.

choices.text: Sign the reply that backs the investment push.
choices.outcome: Two plants and a data centre are brought forward, and growth comes in above forecast. The 20th percentile rises a little, carried along. The other replies go into a drawer.

choices.text: Sign the one for wage support at the bottom.
choices.outcome: Wage support for the lowest-paid goes into the Budget, and their incomes outgrow the median by the next survey. Finance writes, twice, to ask whether the support is temporary.

choices.text: Sign the one that changes nothing.
choices.outcome: The plan that changes nothing changes nothing, on schedule, and the targets are met. Your Permanent Secretary keeps the other two drafts, in a folder marked "Later".

variants.body: The ministry's chief economist has one chart for the next three Budgets: growth strong, incomes at the 20th percentile flat. "You can move either line," the economist says. "Not both, at this price."

choices.text: Move the growth line.
choices.outcome: The growth line climbs above forecast. The 20th-percentile line rises a little too, out of politeness. The economist redraws the chart and labels it "broad-based".

choices.text: Move the 20th-percentile line.
choices.outcome: The lower line overtakes the median's growth, and holds. The economist prints the chart on A3, which economists do not do.

choices.text: Move neither. Hit the targets as planned.
choices.outcome: Both lines stay inside their target bands. The economist calls it the most boring chart of the decade, and is privately proud of it.

variants.body: At a tripartite dinner, a union leader and an employers' federation president sit on either side of you, each with a plan for the next three Budgets. Both plans move the indicators. They move different ones.

choices.text: Back the employers' plan for growth.
choices.outcome: The investment push lands and growth comes in strong. At the next dinner the union leader sits on the other side of the room, and raises a glass to you anyway.

choices.text: Back the union's plan for the lowest-paid.
choices.outcome: Wages at the bottom outgrow the median. The federation's president sends a note of congratulations that is mostly about costs.

choices.text: Back neither. Keep the plan you have.
choices.outcome: Both send notes saying they understand. The targets are met. The two notes are filed together, which neither of them would like.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again
headline.body: Growth is strong again. Your officials bring the plan for the next three Budgets: the last one, which went for the figure everyone watches, with the dates changed in pen. Whatever you sign today, the ministry will roll over from now on.

choices.text: Sign it as it is.
choices.outcome: Signed in pen, beside the old dates. Growth comes in above forecast again, and the Budget debate calls the plan "proven". Nobody asks what else it could have been.

choices.text: Cross it out. Put the 20th percentile first.
choices.outcome: Your officials redraft three years of work in a fortnight, and Finance asks in writing why a plan that was working has changed. Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median by spring.

choices.text: Cross it out. Bank the targets instead.
choices.outcome: The new plan is the old plan with its ambitions removed, and Finance minutes the change as a "recalibration". The targets are met exactly, which the papers report as news.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again
lowest.body: Growth is strong, and the 20th-percentile chart from your last plan now hangs in the ministry lobby, framed. The draft for the next three Budgets keeps it climbing. Nobody expects you to change it, and after this, nobody will ask.

choices.text: Take the chart down. Push headline GDP this time.
choices.outcome: The chart comes down on a Saturday, so nobody sees it go. Growth comes in above forecast, and your chief economist asks, in a long email, what the last three years were for.

choices.text: Sign it. Keep the chart climbing.
choices.outcome: The plan is signed without a meeting. Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median for a second cycle, and the chart in the lobby is replaced by a larger one, which nobody photographs.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Let the chart level off.
choices.outcome: The new plan meets its targets and moves nothing. The chart levels off and comes down, the lobby gets a potted plant, and Finance writes to say it had liked the chart.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again
steady.body: Growth is strong. Last time you chose the safe plan, and it did exactly what it said; other ministries now borrow it. The draft for the next three Budgets is the same plan, and from here it renews itself unless you stop it.

choices.text: Stop it. Push headline GDP while the going is good.
choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast. The ministries that borrowed your plan have to give it back, and your officials rewrite three years of documents in three weeks, without comment.

choices.text: Stop it. Put the 20th percentile first.
choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median by the next survey. The ministries that borrowed your plan ask, in writing, whether they are now meant to change theirs.

choices.text: Let it renew.
choices.outcome: It renews. The targets are met on the decimal, and the plan is cited in a training course as an example of what a plan should be. It is cited nowhere else.

headline: The growth plan is rolled over for three more Budgets, and the quarterly slide keeps its arrow pointing up.
Your officials renew the growth plan without asking, which is what you told them to do, in effect, last time.
Two more plants are brought forward, announced in a press release written from the last one.
In a strong year the plan pushes the figure everyone watches, as it has every year since you signed it.
The growth plan renews itself, and the only edit anyone makes is to the year.
lowest: The plan for the 20th percentile is rolled over for three more Budgets, and the chart in the lobby gets new numbers.
Wage support at the bottom is renewed without a meeting, which is how you can tell it is policy now.
Finance's annual letter asking whether the support for the lowest-paid is temporary arrives on schedule, and is answered from a template.
Your economists print the 20th-percentile chart on A3 again, out of habit.
Another ministry adopts your plan for the lowest incomes, and sends a thank-you note with its own logo on it.
steady: The safe plan is rolled over for three more Budgets, and nobody in the ministry remembers a time before it.
The plan that changes nothing is renewed, unchanged, which is the point of it.
A strong year and a steady plan: the targets are tracked to the decimal place and nothing is announced.
Your officials renew the steady plan, and a training course adds it to its slide titled "Good Practice".
The steady plan renews itself, and its only new feature is a page number.

title: The Indicators, in a Downturn
body: Exports are down for a third quarter and "retrenchment" is back in the papers. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has to be settled now, and the four indicators will measure whatever it achieves.

choices.text: Protect jobs first.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Unemployment rises anyway, by less than it would have. The indicator does not record the difference.

choices.outcome: Unemployment holds. Growth does not. A great many people keep jobs they will never know were on a list.

choices.text: Push growth through it.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The push does not take. Growth is flat and the 20th percentile falls. Nobody calls it a gamble, because it was a plan.

choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region. The speech about resilience writes itself. The jobs come back eighteen months later, in other industries, for other people.

choices.text: Cushion the lowest incomes.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The cushion holds the 20th percentile steady, which is not the same as growing it. The indicator only counts growing.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile hold steady through the downturn, and rent is paid on time in a great many flats. Nobody reports on rent paid on time.

variants.body: The Budget is three weeks away and the downturn is in its fourth quarter. Finance wants each ministry's share of the package by Friday. Your Permanent Secretary has drafted three versions, and has not slept much.

choices.text: Send the wage support, for jobs.
choices.outcome: The wage support goes into the Budget. Firms keep on workers they had already listed, and fill in the forms to say so, in triplicate, grumbling.

choices.text: Send the projects, brought forward.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward and the cranes go up in the west. Growth recovers ahead of the region. Finance's letter of thanks mentions the cranes, twice.

choices.text: Send the cash for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash goes out in March and is spent within a month on rent, school shoes and hawker food. The economists had predicted this to the week.

variants.body: At Tuesday's Meet-the-People Session, three of the first ten cases are retrenchments. On Thursday your ministry settles its plan for the next three Budgets. The three files are still in your bag.

choices.text: Plan for jobs.
choices.outcome: The plan keeps people in work. By spring, retrenchment cases at your Tuesday session are down to one in twenty, and that one wanted to leave anyway.

choices.text: Plan for growth. The jobs will follow it.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region. Two of the three residents find work in the new projects by spring. The third finds it in another industry, and prefers it.

choices.text: Plan for the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes hold steady. The three residents are still looking for work at Chinese New Year, but their rent is paid, and they tell you so, at length.

variants.body: Finance's officials walk you through the downturn package line by line, until they reach your ministry's line, which is blank. Three options are pencilled beside it. Everyone waits, politely, with pens.

choices.text: Write in the jobs scheme.
choices.outcome: The jobs scheme goes in, in ink. Unemployment holds through the downturn. Growth does not, and Finance's officials note this, in pencil.

choices.text: Write in the growth projects.
choices.outcome: The projects go in, in ink, and growth recovers ahead of the region. The other two options are rubbed out by an official with a very good eraser.

choices.text: Write in the cash for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash goes in, in ink, and the lowest incomes hold steady. Finance's officials ask, twice, whether it is temporary. You say yes both times.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
steady.body: Retrenchment is back in the papers. Last time you played it safe, and your officials have drafted the next three Budgets the same way: jobs first, nothing clever. The draft's cover reads "For signature". Not "For decision".

choices.text: Sign it. Jobs first, again.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds through the downturn, as it did last time. The plan is so familiar that the press release is last cycle's, with the year changed by hand.

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward and growth recovers ahead of the region. Your officials, who had expected a signature, spend March rebuilding the plan around cranes.

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Cushion the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash for the lowest incomes goes out in spring, and rent is paid on time in a great many flats. Finance asks, twice, why the plan changed.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
headline.body: Exports have turned down. Last time you went for the figure everyone watches, and your ministry now has a growth unit, with a logo. Its draft for the next three Budgets pushes growth again. The unit would like to continue existing.

choices.text: Overrule the unit. Protect jobs first.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds and growth does not. The growth unit is renamed the Resilience Unit, in a memo that takes eleven drafts, and nobody in it is retrenched.

choices.text: Sign it. The unit knows what it is doing.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region again. The unit's logo goes on the Budget slide, and the papers, which ran this story last time, run a shorter one.

choices.text: Turn the unit to the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The growth unit spends the downturn delivering cash to the lowest incomes, efficiently and with visible reluctance. Rent is paid on time in a great many flats.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
lowest.body: The downturn is official. Last time you put the lowest incomes first, and the payment system built for it is still running, idle, at some expense. Your officials' draft switches it back on. It needs one signature.

choices.text: Repurpose it for wage support, to keep people in work.
choices.outcome: The system is repurposed for wage support, which takes four months and a new acronym. Unemployment holds, and the vendor bills for the acronym.

choices.text: Switch it off. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region on projects brought forward. The idle payment system is finally switched off, and its vendor invoices, politely, for that too.

choices.text: Sign it. Switch it back on.
choices.outcome: The cash goes out within a week, because the system remembered how. The lowest incomes hold steady, and nobody writes about a system that worked twice.

steady: A downturn, and the jobs plan comes out of a folder labelled "Downturn" that nobody has had to look for.
Wage support for jobs is renewed for three more Budgets, and firms fill in the same forms, in triplicate, again.
Retrenchment is back in the papers, and your ministry's jobs scheme is back in the Budget, unchanged.
The downturn plan keeps people in work, announced in last cycle's press release with the year changed.
headline: In a downturn the plan pushes growth through it again, and the cranes go up in the west on schedule.
The growth unit's downturn plan is rolled over, and its logo is redrawn to look more resilient.
Projects are brought forward again, from a list that has not changed since the last downturn.
Exports fall and your ministry pushes growth anyway, reusing the speech about resilience.
lowest: The downturn payment system switches back on for the lowest incomes, and the cash goes out within a week.
Rent is paid on time in a great many flats again, and again nobody reports it.
The plan for the lowest incomes is renewed through the downturn, and Finance asks once, out of habit, whether it is temporary.
The cash goes out in March and is spent by April on rent, school shoes and hawker food, as forecast.

title: The Indicators, Before an Election
body: A general election is due within the year. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets must be settled before Nomination Day, and your branch chairman has sent, unasked, a list of what the ward would like announced.

choices.text: Spread the gains widely before polling day.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The measures land after the indicators are measured. Residents like them anyway; the indicators were not voting.

choices.outcome: The measures land in time and are felt in every block. Your branch chairman reads them out at the CCC dinner, from a printout, with feeling.

choices.text: Hold the line on the targets.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The targets are nearly met. The campaign is a little quieter than your branch would like.

choices.outcome: The targets are met. Your branch chairman asks, politely, whether anything at all could be announced, and is sent the targets.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses its band by a tenth of a point. In an election year, a tenth of a point gets a press conference.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median. The chart is on a campaign flyer by Friday, cropped so the axis starts somewhere encouraging.

variants.body: Your Permanent Secretary briefs you on the next three Budgets and pauses, politely, at the slide titled "Timing". Everyone in the room knows when the election is due. Nobody has said so for forty minutes.

choices.text: Bring everything forward, before polling day.
choices.outcome: The slide titled "Timing" becomes the whole plan. The measures land in time, in every block, and your Permanent Secretary minutes the decision with great care.

choices.text: Keep the timing as it was.
choices.outcome: The plan goes ahead on its original schedule, which falls after polling day. The targets are met. Your branch learns about them from the newspapers, like everyone else.

choices.text: Use the timing for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day. The 20th-percentile chart rises, and is reprinted on a flyer at a size the economists would not approve.

variants.body: The party's election committee asks every office holder for "one thing residents can feel by polling day". Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has three versions. Each would be felt by different residents.

choices.text: Give them something everyone can feel.
choices.outcome: Everyone feels it, briefly. The committee puts it on a poster, and at a walkabout a resident tells you she felt it, and would like it again.

choices.text: Give them the targets, met.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for the targets, met, and asks whether you have anything else. You do not. The committee finds something in another ministry.

choices.text: Give them the lowest incomes, raised.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes rise, and the chart goes on a flyer. Residents who are not on the chart ask what is in it for them. Residents who are on it do not need the flyer.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
headline.body: A general election is due within the year. Your branch has reprinted the last plan's flyer, with the big number in large type, and your officials have drafted the next three Budgets to match. Change it now, or it runs as written.

choices.text: Run it as written.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day, in every block, with the flyer. At a walkabout a resident says it is the same flyer as last time, and she is right.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met and the flyers are pulped. Your branch chairman asks, twice, whether the change could have waited until after polling day, and minutes both answers.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Put the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, and a new flyer is printed with a new chart. The old flyers are used, unofficially, to wrap kueh at the CCC.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
steady.body: Polling day is within the year, and your officials have sent the safe plan again, its annex on timing left blank. Your branch secretary asks, by voice note, what is in it for the ward. Signed, it rolls forward unasked.

choices.text: Fill the annex. Bring the visible measures forward.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day. Your officials redo the annex over a weekend, and Finance asks why a plan that met its targets now needs a timing annex at all.

choices.text: Sign it, blank annex and all.
choices.outcome: The targets are met. Your branch secretary sends a second voice note, which is mostly a sigh, and the campaign leads on the estate's new lifts instead.

choices.text: Fill the annex. The lowest incomes, before polling day.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day. Your branch secretary sends a thumbs-up, the first in three years, and asks for the chart in three more languages.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
lowest.body: Last time you put the lowest incomes first, and the chart has been on campaign flyers ever since. Polling day is within the year. Your officials' draft for the next three Budgets keeps the chart; the covering note calls it "settled policy".

choices.text: Unsettle it. Spread the gains wider before polling day.
choices.outcome: The measures reach every block in time. The chart comes off the flyer, and your officials refile the covering note under a heading that no longer applies.

choices.text: Unsettle it. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, and the flyer has nothing new on it. Your branch chairman reads the covering note aloud at a meeting, slowly, as evidence.

choices.text: Leave it settled.
choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median again. The chart goes on another flyer, and residents who were on it last time say they have seen it.

headline: Before the election, the visible measures are brought forward again, and the flyer is reprinted with a new date.
Polling day approaches and your ministry's measures land in every block, as they did the last time an election was due.
Your branch gets its flyer, its measures and its press conference, in the usual order.
An election year, and the plan is rolled forward to land just before Nomination Day.
steady: An election is due, and the plan holds the line on the targets again; your branch chairman has stopped asking.
The safe plan rolls over into an election year, and your branch learns of it from the newspapers, as usual.
Before polling day your ministry announces nothing new, on schedule.
The targets are kept through another election year, and the campaign leads on lift upgrading instead.
lowest: An election is due, and the 20th-percentile chart goes back on the flyer, cropped as before.
Support for the lowest incomes is timed to land before polling day, as it is every election year now.
Your branch prints the lowest-incomes chart again, and residents on it say they did not need the flyer.
The plan for the lowest incomes renews itself in an election year, and a volunteer translates the chart's caption again.

title: The Recruiter
body: A recruiter has found you on LinkedIn, which you did not know you were still on. A bank would like someone who understands how ministries think. The salary is a number you read twice.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your pass stops working on a Friday. On Monday you have a new one, and a view.

choices.text: Mention the offer, lightly, to HR.
choices.outcome: HR notes your "market value" and, for one ranking cycle, takes you more seriously. It is also noted.

choices.text: Decline. You are not finished here.
choices.outcome: You delete the message. Then you un-delete it, read the number again, and delete it.

title: The Consultancy
body: The firm that charged your ministry $1.9 million for a deck would like to hire someone who knows what ministries actually want. You are that person, apparently. The offer letter is on very good paper.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your first engagement is with your old ministry. The slides are beautiful. They say what your minute papers said.

choices.text: Decline, and tell them why.
choices.outcome: They take it well, and quote you in a thought-leadership piece about public-sector talent.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the letter in a drawer.
choices.outcome: The drawer is the top one. You open it more often than you would admit.

title: The Board Seat
body: A conglomerate would like {post.ask} on its board: four meetings a year, and a fee the annual report puts in a footnote. Its chairman knows you hold office. He asks only whether you might be free "after".

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} At the election a new candidate wins your seat. The board seat was, as promised, kept warm.

choices.text: Decline.
choices.outcome: You decline in writing, which you will later find was framed in the chairman's office as a curiosity.

options.ask: someone who has worked close to Cabinet
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.
options.exit: The Prime Minister asks you to see out the term, and you do.

options.ask: someone who has run part of a ministry
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.

options.ask: someone who has sat in Cabinet

options.exit: The reshuffle announcement thanks you in its second paragraph.

variants.body: At a charity dinner, a chairman you have met twice steers you to the window. His board needs {post.ask}, at a time that suits you. He names the fee quietly, then again, in case you were being polite.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} A new candidate holds your seat. Flowers arrive at your first board meeting, a quarter of your working year.

choices.text: Thank him, and decline.
choices.outcome: You decline at the window, smiling. He says the offer will keep, and every Chinese New Year a card arrives to show that it is keeping.

variants.body: A search firm writes on paper thick enough to stand up by itself. A board seat, for {post.ask}, from "a date convenient to you". The fee is in the second paragraph, which is short.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} Your seat passes to a new candidate. The search firm's next letter begins "Dear Director", and is much thinner.

choices.text: Decline, on your own letterhead.
choices.outcome: The search firm replies within the hour, thanking you, and files you under "later". The list is long, and attentive.
